Vijayadaśamī
------------------------------------------
Festivals and sacred days observed by the Hindus are not only days of personal austerity but also occasions for joyous reunions.
One of the most popular of such festivals is the विजयदशमी (the tenth day in the bright half of the month of Āśvayuja or Āśvina in September/October). It is considered one of the three most auspicious of the days in the year. It is on this day that images of मोथेर् दुर्गा, worshipped during the नवरात्र festival are ceremonially immersed in water. (See DURGĀPŪJĀ.)
Śrī राम is said to have killed रावण on this day and got victory. Hence it came to be known as विजयदशमी (Daśamī of Victory).
See also NAVARĀTRA.

vijñāna
(‘special knowledge’)
------------------------------------------
This word has been used in several senses. In the Bhagavadgītā (18-42) it means experience of the higher truths. The पुराणस् use the word to indicate fourteen kinds of विद्यास् or areas of knowledge such as the वेदस्, वेदाङ्गस्, Mīmāṁsā and the पुराणस्. It may also mean arts and sciences like architecture, इचोनोग्रफ्य् and so on. विज्ञान is also interpreted as memorising a treatise and understanding it thoroughly.

------------------------------------------
Great saints have often shown that they have extraordinary powers of intuition and prediction. पुरन्दरदास (A.

-1564), one of the great vaiṣṇava saints of Karnataka, had foretold that his last son Madhvapati would have to be reborn to complete his own mission of composing many more devotional songs which he could not do. The Haridāsa tradition of Karnataka (See DĀSAKŪṬA.) believes that विजयदास was the reincarnation of Madhvapati.
VijayadāsaBorn as the eldest son of Sīnappa and Kūsamma at Cīkalapari (in the Raichur district of Karnataka) विजय-dāsa’s original name was Dāsappa. He grew in that village without much एदुचतिओन्, into a young man. Poverty and selfishness of the people around him as also the arrogance of his own rich uncle, forced him to abandon his होउसे and walk all the way to काशी. There, on the bank of the river गङ्गा, when he fell asleep, the saint पुरन्दरदास is said to have appeared in his dream and initiated him, instantly converting him into the sage विजयदास.
He toured the country extensively, mostly in Southern India, तिरुपति and उडुपि being his favourite places of पिल्ग्रिमगे.
Among his disciples, the following became more well-known in course of time:
Gopāladāsa, Veṇugopāladāsa, Mohana-dāsa, Śeṣagiridāsa, Vyāsaviṭṭhaladāsa and Ānandadāsa.
Vijayadāsa has left a very large number of devotional songs, especially of a particular type called ‘suḷādi’. The language is simple and generally deals with such topics as greatness of God’s divine name, need for the grace of the गुरु and God, importance of ज्ञान (know-ledge), भक्ति (devotion) and वैराग्य (renunciation) in spiritual life and God as Śrīhari or Hari (Viṣṇu/Nārāyaṇa), the greatest of all gods. He has given quite a bit of information in his compositions about पुरन्दरदास and his contemporaries that help us to get historical details about them.

Vijñāneśvara
------------------------------------------
If it is possible for a treatise to be more celebrated than its author, there can be no better example than विज्ञानेश्वर and his Mitākṣarā (his commentary on the Yājñavalkya Smṛti).
He must have composed his work during the period A.

-1120.
He was the son of Padmanābha भट्ट and a pupil of Uttama. He composed his work during the reign of the king Vikramārka or Vikramādityadeva (A.

-1126) in the city of Kalyāṇa. He had embraced monastic life.
He was a great scholar in the Pūrva-mīmāṁsā philosophy, the rules of which he has often applied while determining the meaning of certain statements.
See also MITĀKṢARĀ.

)
------------------------------------------
Vijñānabhikṣu is a well-known and prolific writer, especially on the Sāṅkhya and योग philosophies. Except that he was a saṁnyāsin (monk) and probably lived in काशी, nothing else is known about him. Some hazard the guess that he was originally from Bengal. However, there is no clinching evidence to prove it.
The following are his works:
Vijñānāmṛtabhāṣyam (on the Brahma-sūtras); Yogavārttika (commentary on the Vyāsabhāśya of the Yogasūtras of पतञ्जलि [200 B. C.]); Sāṅkhyapravacanabhāṣya (commentary on the Sāñkhyasūtras of कपिल); Yogasārasaṅgraha (an independent treatise giving the summary of the Yoga-sūtras); Sāṅkhyasāra (similar work on Sāṅkhya philosophy).
Some of the works ascribed to him and not yet published are:
Commentaries on some उपनिषद्स्; Pāṣaṇḍamatakhaṇḍanam; Brahmādarśa; Vaiśeṣikadarśanavārttikam; and Īśvara-gītābhāṣya (on the Gītā taken from the Kūrmapurāṇa).
His interpretation of the Brahma-sūtras is nearer to theistic Sāṅkhya.

vijātīyabheda
(‘difference based on different species’)
------------------------------------------
Bheda or difference is one of the concepts discussed in the Vedāntic treatises to establish the nature of the ultimate realities. It is generally classified into three varieties: सजातीयभेद; vijātīya-bheda; स्वगतभेद.
A cow and a horse are different from one another because they belong to different jātis or categories. This is an example of विजातीयभेद.
Among a number of cows, one cow is different from another cow. This is an example of सजातीयभेद or difference within the same category.
Within the body of a cow, the horns, the legs, the tail and the ears are all different from one another. This is the example for स्वगतभेद or internal differences.
The Viśiṣṭādvaita Vedānta of Rāmānuja (A.

-1137) does not accept the first two kinds of bhedas in ब्रह्मन् but accepts the third. According to this, the jīvas (individual souls which are infinite in number) and the प्रकृति (insentient nature)—these two also called cit (conscious entity) and अचित् (unconscious matter)—are internal parts of ईश्वर or ब्रह्मन्.
